title: Fewer approval clicks. Same ability to catch mistakes?
summary: Test whether showing the consequences of an AI-proposed change makes human review easier without hiding errors.
contribution: An experiment design and reusable review tasks—not another agent framework.
feasibility: Start with fictional ticket-routing changes. A later study needs participants and supervisor agreement.
venture: An approval interface for small automation teams. Buyer demand is untested.
next: Create six example cases and a feasible evaluation plan before recruiting anyone.
evidence: Adjacent research exists; this specific comparison still needs a prior-work check.
question: Can consequence summaries reduce review effort while preserving consequential-error detection?
measure: Errors caught · review time · perceived effort
risk: Faster approval could mean less scrutiny.
alternative: Ordinary diffs, approval dialogs and checklists
reason: Closest match to your interest in approval fatigue.

title: The AI was right. Did the workflow still fail?
summary: Separate a wrong AI answer from a correct answer delivered twice, sent to the wrong place, or never completed.
contribution: A fault-labelled trace benchmark comparing output checks with execution checks.
feasibility: Use small synthetic traces on a laptop. Real-system validation would be a later step.
venture: A testing component for automation builders. Existing evaluation tools are strong alternatives.
next: Define a trace format, twelve examples and a baseline comparison.
evidence: n8n already offers evaluations; operational complaints motivate investigation but do not prove a research gap.
question: Do execution invariants detect failures that output-only evaluations miss?
risk: Could reduce to ordinary systems testing rather than an AI thesis.
alternative: n8n evaluations, logs and unit tests
reason: Strong engineering fit; does not need participant recruitment.

title: When your smart home should say “I’m not sure”
summary: Study how occupancy estimates should behave when room sensors and the total number of people disagree.
contribution: A robustness study of probabilistic estimates and an explicit unknown state.
feasibility: Begin with a three-room simulation. No sensors or real household monitoring required.
venture: More understandable home automation. Consumer demand and energy savings are not established.
next: Specify three baselines and ten sensor-conflict examples.
evidence: Home Assistant already supports Bayesian sensor fusion. The possible gap is robustness to contradictory signals.
question: When do whole-home constraints help, and when is an unknown answer safer?
risk: A favourable simulator may not reflect real homes.
alternative: Bayesian sensors, timers and manual overrides
reason: An outside-software-industry option with an Applied AI core.

title: Replay a workflow failure—and see what went wrong
summary: Drop a small execution trace into a browser and see duplicate actions, missing completion events and broken steps.
contribution: A visual timeline and an exportable incident report using six sample failures.
feasibility: One local web page, one JSON format, no accounts or integrations.
venture: Potential debugging aid for solo automation builders. Willingness to pay is unknown.
next: Build the sample-trace viewer, verify each failure and publish a small demo.
evidence: Workflow evaluations already exist. The test is whether this makes a failure easier to understand.
question: Can you understand a workflow incident faster than by reading raw logs?
risk: May offer little beyond a good log viewer.
alternative: n8n logs, JSON viewers and custom scripts
reason: Recommended for a small, testable first engineering release.

title: Why did changing my food preferences do nothing?
summary: Show how food preferences affect a comparison—and explain ties, missing information and unchanged rankings.
contribution: A comparison demo with twelve fictional products and transparent score contributions.
feasibility: Use fictional products and simple non-medical preferences. No food API or nutritional advice.
venture: An explanation feature for shopping apps. One complaint is not proof of a market.
next: Create six preference-change scenarios and a clear side-by-side comparison.
evidence: One reported issue plus existing Open Food Facts matching APIs; the cause of that issue is unconfirmed.
question: Is explaining an unchanged result more useful than a simple product filter?
measure: Six hand-checked scenarios · clear unknown states
risk: A plain attribute table might explain it better.
alternative: Product filters and Open Food Facts matching
reason: A small consumer-facing alternative with no AI dependency.

title: An annual bill is not always “divide by twelve”
summary: Explain the difference between a bill’s monthly average and what you need to put aside before its due date.
contribution: A household timeline with six fictional bills, reserves and transparent calculations.
feasibility: A local page with deterministic arithmetic; no bank connection or real financial records.
venture: A household planning utility or existing-app feature. Spreadsheet substitution is strong.
next: Build the timeline and verify six date, reserve and rounding cases.
evidence: A forum question title is a lead only; the underlying discussion has not yet been verified.
question: Does a timeline explain irregular bills better than a spreadsheet?
measure: Correct dates · exact rounding · understandable amounts
risk: The problem may already be solved well by spreadsheets.
alternative: Spreadsheets, savings pots and budgeting apps
reason: Quick to test with a familiar consumer problem.
